sources.title: Thomas W. Kavanagh: Comanche, Oklahoma Historical Society
sources.note: Direct text read. Early 1700s New Mexico presence; fluid organization, extended families, councils and 1966 constitution. Date and polygon warning is our comparison with decoded map.

sources.title: National Park Service: Comanches and Horses
sources.note: Direct text, paragraphs on early eighteenth-century horse economy, trade, camps and overgrazing. Based on Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire.

sources.title: Smithsonian: Comanche cradleboard, NMAI 22897
sources.note: Exact indexed museum record read; direct object opening failed. Collected from Ta-ki-ti in Oklahoma in 1909; materials and techniques. Collection date is not manufacture date.

sources.title: National Museum of the American Indian: Parfleche bag, 2/1840
sources.note: Direct catalogue: collected from Koma in 1909, Oklahoma, rawhide and paint.

sources.title: Comanche Nation: Language
sources.note: Official page, Mission: exact modern Comanche sentence and supplied English translation. Accessed September 2026; no ancient inscription claimed.

sources.title: Comanche Nation: Summer Youth Program Hosts TEK Camp
sources.note: Official report, interviews with campers and coordinators. No year assumed from undated page; explicitly modern programming.

sources.title: Comanche Nation: Fair Brings Back Buffalo Butchering
sources.note: Official event report: children helping, bones for tools, relationship with Cheyenne-Arapaho buffalo programme. No universal custom inferred.

sources.title: National Park Service: Comanche, Fort Davis
sources.note: Direct article: 1874 to 1875 Red River War and forced reservation settlement.

sources.title: University of Arizona: Comanche Nation Constitution
sources.note: Native Nations Institute catalogue: constitution dated 1966, amended later; evidence of continuing self-government.

sources.title: John H. Moore: Southern Cheyenne, Oklahoma Historical Society
sources.note: Direct article. Minnesota background, eighteenth-century migration, horse economy and later confinement. Dated article not used for current membership figures or government structure.

sources.title: Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes: Language and Culture
sources.note: Direct tribal page: Cheyenne history, crops, modern classes and exact Tsistsistas translation. Its community translation is attributed; older Moore article regards etymology as uncertain.

sources.title: W. Raymond Wood: Biesterfeldt, Smithsonian Contributions to Anthropology 15
sources.note: Direct 1971 scholarly abstract. Approximately sixty earth lodges, central plaza, c.1750 to 1790, pottery and explicitly circumstantial Cheyenne identification.

sources.title: National Park Service: Hunting and Processing Bison Robes
sources.note: Direct resource study adaptation. Garrard observed Cheyenne women in 1846 to 1847; stretching, scraping and softening; robes fully processed for trade.

sources.title: Smithsonian: Northern Cheyenne hide scraper, 10/4474
sources.note: Exact indexed original catalogue read; direct failed. Lame Deer attribution, elk bone, hide ties and metal. Earlier collection history unknown; lent 1921 and donated 1925.

sources.title: National Museum of the American Indian: Cup and pin game
sources.note: Direct museum record: Northern Cheyenne, Montana, deer bone, strung; collected from Little White Man in 1924 or 1925. Rules not supplied, so not reconstructed.

sources.title: History Colorado: Cheyenne Dog Soldier Ledgerbook
sources.note: Direct collection interpretation: 106 coloured-pencil drawings by fourteen artists, 1864 to 1869 events, recovered at Summit Springs. Pictorial narrative, not claimed as phonetic writing.

sources.title: National Park Service: Bent’s New Fort and Fort Wise/Lyon
sources.note: Direct NPS account: November 29, 1864 attack on peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho village. Approximate casualty estimates avoided.

sources.title: Montana Office of Public Instruction: Northern Cheyenne Reservation Timeline
sources.note: Direct five-page PDF: 1878 flight, 1880 settlement, 1884 reservation. Modern Northern identity distinct from Southern nation.

sources.title: Northern Cheyenne Tribe: Public Information
sources.note: Official contemporary government document index in Lame Deer; constitutional, water, court and council documents show continuing government.

sources.title: Florida Museum: Investigating the Calusa
sources.note: Direct museum research report: Mound Key king-house excavation, construction phases, fish bones and watercourts dated 1300 to 1400. Capacity of 2,000 is from Spanish accounts, not excavated headcount.

sources.title: Randell Research Center: Calusa chronology
sources.note: Direct chronology: regional archaeological phases and Spanish contacts 1513, 1521, 1566 to 1569; slave raids and eighteenth-century refugees.

sources.title: Karen Walker: Did the Calusa Have a Great Fishery of Mullet?
sources.note: Direct researcher account, December 2019 newsletter: reassessment of bone samples, sampling and identification biases; strongest late signal at Mound Key.

sources.title: John Dietler: Economic Stimulus Package, A.D. 800
sources.note: Direct researcher report of 441 woodworking tools from 93 sites, shell workshops and radiocarbon dates. Interpretation of political control explicitly remains hypothesis.

sources.title: Florida Museum: The Key Marco Collection
sources.note: Direct museum collection account, 1896 wet-site excavation, netting, gauges, wood, masks and domestic vessels.

sources.title: Smithsonian: Key Marco Cat, object and research notes
sources.note: Catalogue supplies varying published dates: 1400 to 1500 in 1985 publication, broader 700 to 1500 in 2012. Maker may be Calusa or predecessor; broad uncertainty preserved. No reliance on outdated loan-status field.

sources.title: Randell Research Center: Tracking the Calusa Overseas
sources.note: Direct first-person archival research report, December 2002: 1711 mixed refugee group and 1760 departures; original documents in Seville and Cuban historical sites.

sources.title: Randell Research Center: Irma’s Impacts
sources.note: Direct research-centre article explicitly says Calusa and ancestors left no written records; distinction from Spanish testimony retained.

sources.title: National Park Service: The Ancestral Sonoran Desert People
sources.note: Direct text. Archaeological term rather than single tribe, red-on-buff pottery by 450, Classic period through about 1450, crops, settlement changes and living descendants.

sources.title: S’edav Va’aki Museum: Outdoor Trails
sources.note: Direct museum interpretation: gradient and erosion/silt, canals, ballcourts and uncertainty over their exact use. Avoids unsupportable superlative largest in entire New World.

sources.title: Pueblo Grande Museum: Hohokam Houses teacher guide
sources.note: Direct 13-page PDF: pages 4 to 8, floor evidence, courtyard clusters, inferred extended-family cooperation, grinding equipment. Reconstruction distinguished from observation.

sources.title: National Park Service: Engineered to Last
sources.note: Direct wayside interpretation: caliche composition, water mixing and successive courses visible in Great House walls.

sources.title: National Park Service: Arizona, Casa Grande Ruins
sources.note: Indexed official original text: Great House completed about 1350; timbers from up to sixty miles away; internal beams and saguaro ribs.

sources.title: Chris Lange: Ancient Technologies, Hohokam Etched Shell
sources.note: Direct shell specialist report, November 19, 2024. Snaketown unfinished horned-lizard design with resist in place, dominant Sacaton contexts 950 to 1150. Fermented cactus juice proposed, not chemically proven for each artifact.

sources.title: National Park Service: Casa Grande History and Culture
sources.note: Direct page: archaeological label, disuse about 1450 and no written language left behind; written visitor record begins with Kino in 1694.

sources.title: S’edav Va’aki Museum: Plan Your Visit
sources.note: Direct/indexed official museum account: after 1400 population declined and moved to smaller villages; Akimel O’odham descendants continue in Phoenix region.

batchIdentityNotes.assessment: Decoded first polygon in world-1500 spans roughly 103.00W to 94.84W and 28.30N to 33.73N, central/southern Texas. Its 1500 placement predates documented early-eighteenth-century southern expansion. Public opening explicitly warns. Map interval 1500 to 1783 retained as coverage only; later dated objects and events remain visibly later. No aliases or successors proposed.

First decoded 1492 polygon spans 111.53W to 99.10W and 37.54N to 48.08N, far west of the earlier Minnesota setting. Public opening flags the anachronistic outline. No map-year attribution of nineteenth-century materials. Biesterfeldt identification qualified, contemporary Northern and Southern institutional identities distinguished. Community self-name translation explicitly attributed because Moore treats its etymology as uncertain.

Decoded 1492 outline covers southwest/southern Florida, approximately 82.75W to 80.60W and 25.12N to 27.74N. Appropriate regional identity, no claim exact border. Map period 1492 to 1530 is coverage only. Early workshop evidence and uncertain Key Marco attribution are explicitly contextual, not proof a single kingdom existed unchanged since 800. No modern descendant association or successor invented.

Decoded 1492 outline spans southern/central Arizona, approximately 113.05W to 109.86W and 31.48N to 35.44N. Geographic fit is broad but imported 1492 to 1500 interval postdates conventional c.1450 archaeological endpoint. Public opening and period both warn. No single tribe, extinct people or invasion inferred; no cross-association with Hopi/Zuni/O’odham solely on ancestry. NPS sources vary early starting date, so not offered as a precise founding date.
